chapter: Coming up in New York and Harlem theatres
title: Writing 'I'd Do Almost Anything for You' and giving it to Claude Hopkins
summary: Whaley wrote the number by reversing 'Nagasaki', gave the orchestration to Claude Hopkins, who published it as his theme, and he got nothing.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: See, so Claude came by the theatre and say hey Tom, give me that orchestration and I'll play it down at Roseland and I said oh, we played it enough and put it on a chair and Carey said, yeah, give it to him and let him play it down there, so me, like a fool, give it to him and within six weeks he had had it published. Joe Williams wrote the words.

No, Bill Williams. He used to write lyrics and Joe Page or Joe Daley was the publisher and Claude Hopkins wrote the music, and I said to Claude, 'you should give me $100 for that tune?' I said, 'that made you. You took that as your theme song.' 'I would swim the ocean wide, I would cross that great divide. I'd do almost anything for you.' I says 'how we come to write that, Carey said we got to have a jump number and I was playing (humming) and I started just putting it backwards. Oomphaing it, and I said, I got it (humming).'
That's what you did, you took that and played it backwards. So 'Nagasaki' backwards, I would do most anything for you.
That's right, so -- I always call him Joe, it's Bill Williams, he wrote the lyrics and it became --

oh, Bill Robinson's, Charlie -- all of them guy were singing it and the people were coming out the doors and they'd stop and the guy would say, what's going on, they're having a good time on my number and sure enough, that was a big number.
Beautiful. You feel like taking a little breather for a minute.
